questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
questions.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z+4}{3}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-(-4)}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(3,1,-4)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,1,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
questions.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=5+5t \\ z=-1+6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ 5+5t \\ -1+6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ 6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,5,-1)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z+1}{6}.
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=-3+5t \\ z=7-6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ -3+5t \\ 7-6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ -6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(2,-3,7)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,-6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-(-3)}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y+3}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-3)}{0}=\frac{y-5}{-2}=\frac{z-0}{1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+3}{0}=\frac{y-5}{-2}=z,
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+3}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-3:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5-2t \\ t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+3}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-3,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{y-5}{-2}=z,\,x=-3
$$

We know that the line passes through the points $P(7,-2,4)$ and $Q(1,1,4).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$

$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-4}{0}.

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{z-4}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=4.$ For example, our two points $P(7,-2,4)$ and $Q(1,1,4)$ both have $z$-coordinates of $z=4.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-4}{0}$ part and instead write $z=4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y+2}{3},\,z=4

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\dfrac{x}{5}=\dfrac{y+3}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{1}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x}=\dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y}=\dfrac{z-z_0}{v_z} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\dfrac{x}{5}=\dfrac{y-(-3)}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{1},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(0,-3,2)$ and is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=\langle 5,3,1 \rangle.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

{\begin{aligned}x=1-2t \\ y=4t \\ z=-2+3t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-2t \\ 4t \\ -2+3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2t \\ 4t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(1,0,-2)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle -2, 4, 3 \rangle.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{-2}=\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{z-(-2)}{3} = t, 	\qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{-2}=\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{z+2}{3}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14042625/assets/fea24c391122278ffe20ec0f6a7d704b835aca18c3bdcd7395aeeea0f593a2bf.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-3}{5} = t,	\qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-3}{5},
$$

which is problematic because $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14042625/assets/368f42200b9366547bdff9840a894b63d3df43722052ecb1a4e15e2306b4e56a.png)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{z-3}{5}, \; y=2
$$
